html:
The war of 1965 was the second war between India and Pakistan over Kashmir. It lasted seven weeks and ended in a draw that hurt Pakistan more.

Pakistan's leaders judged that India was weak after its defeat by China in 1962 (see the Sino-Indian War) and the death of Nehru. In August 1965 they sent several thousand armed men across the ceasefire line into Indian-held Kashmir, expecting the people to rise. They did not; villagers reported the men to the army.

On 1 September Pakistani tanks struck toward the one road linking Kashmir to India. The Indian prime minister, Lal Bahadur Shastri, answered on 6 September by sending the army across the international border toward Lahore. Pakistan had not expected that. The tank battles that followed in Punjab were among the largest since 1945.

Both sides were running short of ammunition when the United Nations arranged a ceasefire on 23 September. The Soviet Union brought the two leaders together at Tashkent in January 1966, and they agreed to go back to the old lines. Shastri died there of a heart attack hours after signing.

In Pakistan the result discredited the military ruler Ayub Khan (see the 1958 coup). East Pakistan, left almost undefended, drew its own lessons (see the war of 1971).
sum: The war of 1965 was the second war between India and Pakistan over Kashmir. It lasted seven weeks and ended in a draw that hurt Pakistan more.
